title: Atisha comes
hookLine: the Indian master Atisha arrives and renews the teaching

cards: In the far west of Tibet, a royal family wants the teaching back, and done properly. Tibetans tell a story about one of these kings, Yeshe O.

Tradition says he was captured by an enemy while gathering gold to invite a great teacher from India. When his family raised his ransom, he sent word back: don't spend it on me. Use it to bring the teacher.
He died in captivity, the story says, and the invitation went on without him.

teach.b: The teacher was Atisha, an Indian master from the monastery of Vikramashila. Tradition says he was reluctant, and that his own abbot didn't want to let him go.
But he came over the mountains, and he stayed in Tibet for the rest of his life.
What he found, the accounts say, was a teaching that had scattered. Some people kept the rules and looked down on meditation. Others claimed secret practices and let ethics slide.
So Atisha wrote a short text for the Tibetans: A Lamp for the Path to Enlightenment. Its gift is order.
It sorts practitioners by what they're aiming for: some for a better life to come, some for their own freedom, some to free all beings.

teach.h: EACH STAGE RESTS ON THE LAST.
teach.b: And the path rises in stages, each resting on the one before: ethics, then meditation, then wisdom, with compassion running through all of it. Nothing thrown away. Everything in its place.
Atisha also taught ways of training the mind: turning everyday trouble into practice, and putting others before yourself.
His student Dromtonpa gathered his followers into the Kadam school, and later Tibetan schools built on his Lamp.

So this is what renewal looked like. Not a new religion, and not a return to exactly what was lost. A teacher who came in, listened, saw what had scattered, and lit a lamp so the pieces could be found again.

how: Tibetan Buddhists study Atisha's Lamp for the Path and the stages-of-the-path teachings built on it, and practice mind training, which traces its lineage to Atisha.

games.q: you're King Yeshe O, held captive. your family has raised gold for your ransom. what do you do?
o: take the ransom and go home.
tell them to spend it on inviting the teacher.
tell them to raise an army.
games.why: tradition says he sent word: don't spend it on me, bring the teacher. he died in captivity, and the invitation went on.

practice: Bring to mind something that once mattered and has scattered, a habit, a friendship, a practice, a hope, and with no scolding, picture lighting one small lamp beside it, enough to see where the pieces are.
Ask what one first step back would look like, then rest with the breath, steady as a small flame.

wordCard.voice: Atisha comes. The Indian master Atisha arrives in Tibet and renews the teaching, putting the path back in order with his Lamp.

orig.note: Sanskrit pradipa, lamp. Atisha's Lamp for the Path is known in Sanskrit as the Bodhipathapradipa.

carryVoice: Your line: the renewal. A king's ransom, spent on a teacher instead. See you tomorrow.
